issues.legal_issue: An assessment rule that takes effect during an agricultural year applies to an assessment for the whole year that is made after the rule takes effect.
material_facts: The tax assessment covered the agricultural year from 1 July 1957 to 30 June 1958.
The assessment was made after the relevant rule took effect on 23 April 1958.
The assessment concerned the entire agricultural year and was made pursuant to a notice served while the year was still in progress.
issues.conclusion: The rule applied to the pending assessment for the entire agricultural year, even though the year began before the rule took effect.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Large Land Holdings Tax Act, 1957 provide for tax on the annual value of a landholding for the agricultural year and define the landholding and its annual value. Section 29 authorises rules to carry out the Act's purposes. The Court treated the rules governing assessment and computation as procedural, and held that a rule effective during the assessment year applies to an assessment for that whole year made after the rule takes effect. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.tax_assessment_proceeding: An authority assessed tax on a person's landholding.
predicates.assessment_covers_entire_agricultural_ye: The assessment covered the whole agricultural year rather than only a period after the rule took effect.
predicates.assessment_rule_is_procedural: The rule governed the conduct or computation of the assessment.
predicates.rule_took_effect_before_assessment_was_m: The rule took effect before the authority made the assessment.

issues.definition: When a procedural rule takes effect before a tax assessment covering an entire agricultural year is made, the rule applies to that full-year assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A landholder's attainment of majority during the assessment year does not defeat relief for land legally sublet while the landholder was disabled.
material_facts: The landholder was a minor until 3 March 1958 and attained majority on 4 March 1958.
The land was sublet to tenants under the orders of the Court of Wards and, later, the District Judge while the properties were under their management.
The landholder claimed relief for the sublet land in an assessment for the agricultural year ending 30 June 1958.
issues.conclusion: Attaining majority before the end of the assessment year did not deprive the landholder of the rule's benefit for land legally sublet while the landholder was disabled.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 6-A of the Uttar Pradesh Large Land Holdings Rules, 1957 provides for remission of holding tax on land legally sublet by a disabled landholder of the kind described in section 157(1) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. The Court read the rule as attaching the benefit to land that had been legally sublet, rather than requiring the landholder to remain a minor through the assessment year. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.tax_assessment_proceeding: An authority assessed tax on a person's landholding.
predicates.land_was_legally_sublet_by_a_disabled_la: A landholder who was disabled under the relevant land law legally sublet the land.
predicates.landholder_attained_majority_during_asse: The landholder attained majority before the assessment year ended.

issues.definition: If a disabled landholder legally sublets land and attains majority during the assessment year, that change in status does not defeat the relief claimed for the sublet land.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not raise on appeal a challenge to the legality of subletting that it did not dispute in the High Court.
material_facts: The landholder relied on the legal subletting of the land in the High Court.
The State did not dispute the legality of the subletting there.
The State raised the legality of the subletting as a ground in its appeal.
issues.conclusion: The State could not raise the legality of the subletting for the first time on appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a party that did not dispute the legality of the subletting in the High Court could not raise that contention on appeal. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this point.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_decision: A party appealed a decision made by a High Court.
predicates.legality_of_subletting_was_not_disputed_: The party did not contest the legality of the subletting in the High Court.
predicates.party_challenges_legality_on_appeal: The party challenged the legality of the subletting in the appeal.

issues.definition: When a party did not dispute the legality of subletting in the High Court but challenges it on appeal, the appellate challenge is not entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may issue a writ where the dispute concerns the construction of a statute or assessment rules, even if the alleged error is not patent.
material_facts: The landholder challenged the assessment authorities' application of the assessment rule in a writ petition.
The challenge concerned the construction of the statute and rules governing assessment.
The State argued that the High Court could not issue a writ because the error was not patent.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in issuing a writ because the dispute concerned the construction of the statute and assessment rules.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the application of the statute and rules in an assessment as a question of construction and held that the High Court was justified in issuing a writ on that basis; it rejected the argument that the error had to be patent. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.writ_challenges_tax_assessment: A person sought a writ challenging a tax assessment.
predicates.dispute_requires_construction_of_assessm: Resolving the challenge required construing the law governing the assessment.
predicates.assessment_authority_misconstrued_that_l: The authority applied the assessment law on an incorrect construction.

issues.definition: When a writ challenge to a tax assessment turns on the assessment authority's incorrect construction of the governing law, the High Court may issue a writ.
